source.title: Synthetic Benchmarks Overstate Forward-Forward Scaling: Real-Data Limits of Layer-Local Training

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no garbling or cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates Forward-Forward against backpropagation mainly using test accuracy and systems measurements. Its synthetic training-accuracy results do not test the listed CIFAR CNN, depth, initialization, learning-rate, or normalization claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own synthetic teacher–student training-accuracy comparison, but it is not one of the listed benchmark or architectural settings. CIFAR and ImageNet results are test accuracies, so they do not establish training classification error. Mentioned prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests Forward-Forward scaling, not any listed version. Its training-accuracy results concern synthetic multilayer perceptrons rather than CIFAR convolutional networks. Its depth and normalization comparisons report test accuracy, without the training-error, training-speed, or learning-rate measurements the versions require.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that their strong DTG-FF implementation still trails architecture-matched BP on real images, while synthetic class-count sweeps give an advantage that reverses on real data. Synthetic DTG-FF also fits training data less closely. Their systems audit finds that pipelined FF's activation-memory property does not deliver practical dominance over BP with gradient accumulation on the tested hardware. They present cross-layer coordination as an interpretation, not a causally established explanation.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares layer-local Forward-Forward training with backpropagation; it does not reproduce the listed claims’ interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: On synthetic tasks, the relative DTG-FF versus BP-DeepSup test-accuracy result varies with class count K; on real images the gap reverses and widens with K. CIFAR-100 coarse and fine label granularity also changes the reported test-accuracy gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic BP students fit training data nearly perfectly, whereas DTG-FF reaches approximately 86–97% training accuracy for K≥10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these synthetic multilayer teacher–student tasks, detached layer-local training fits the training set less closely than end-to-end backpropagation.

fits_no_version.finding: DTG-FF VGG11 has lower test accuracy than VGG8 by 6.97 points on CIFAR-10 and 12.49 points on CIFAR-100; depth, early width, and downsampling differ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested deeper, narrower DTG-FF architecture generalizes worse on CIFAR; the comparison does not isolate depth or establish training-error degradation.

record.problems: The benchmark accuracies are selected as the best official-test-split results during training. The synthetic training-accuracy summary is a range across K without per-K values in the prose. The paper states that both CIFAR-100 coarse/fine runs are non-converged at 50 epochs and that the probe is direction-suggestive rather than asymptotic.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows: the study's CIFAR, ImageNet, and secondary-benchmark figures report test accuracy rather than training classification error; systems measurements and cited prior-work results do not measure a version's named behavior.

untested.parts: CIFAR-10/100 CNN training classification error, including corrupted labels and model-size, early-stopping, and regularization conditions.
Two-layer teacher–student width scaling, spurious-minimum frequency, and adding one or two student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts; special-initialization and normalization-free residual comparisons.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, training speed, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery or divergence, and sharpness dynamics.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance; Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply. Normalization ablations measure final test accuracy, not V6's training acceleration; the depth comparison likewise cannot establish V3. States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions, despite readable training-accuracy values.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 CNN training error, random or corrupted labels, and effects of model size, early stopping, and regularization.
Teacher–student width scaling and spurious-minimum frequency.
Plain versus residual network training error by depth, and the stated special-initialization and normalization comparisons.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery or divergence, and sharpness dynamics.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup comparisons.

rows.subject: BP
rows.operation_detail: End-to-end cross-entropy training on synthetic teacher–student data; training accuracy summarized for K ≥ 10.
rows.value: near-100% training accuracy at all K ≥ 10
rows.locator: Appendix E, Train–test gap analysis; Table 5
rows.note: Synthetic MLP result; the text gives a qualitative summary rather than individual training-accuracy values.
rows.check: The qualitative value is correct, but per-K mean training accuracies can be reconstructed from Table 5: 99.9%, 99.9%, 99.8%, 99.4%, and 100.0% for K=10,15,20,30,50. These synthetic MLP results do not measure V1's CIFAR CNN claim or V2's width-dependent spurious minima.

rows.subject: DTG-FF
rows.operation_detail: Layer-local training on synthetic teacher–student data; training accuracy summarized for K ≥ 10.
rows.locator: Appendix E, Train–test gap analysis; Table 5
rows.note: The text gives a range across K, not separate values for each K.
rows.check: The qualitative range is correct, but Table 5 permits per-K reconstruction: 96.7%, 95.9%, 94.0%, 86.1%, and 91.2% for K=10,15,20,30,50. Appendix E specifies detached layer-local cross-entropy on squared activations with fixed random readouts. This does not measure any listed version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
